text: A pen is a hard thing to photograph, and Thomas Paine's entire action was a pen. Haskell Wexler gives the life seventy-three minutes: a revolution in America set alight, another in France given its language, Reason argued in print by a man who kept moving between the two. The compression is where the interest sits. At that length nothing can be lingered over, so the film has to decide what a pamphlet does in the hours after it lands and put that on screen instead of rooms and dates. Paine survives mostly as sentences, and sentences do not move on their own; the work falls to voice, to pacing, to where a camera can stand while an argument is read out. Made in 1982, it takes the writing to be the event and not the decoration around one.

The auditor comes back every night and asks for the same dancer. Atom Egoyan arranges Exotica as a circuit of people looking at someone who will not look back: Francis at Christina, the MC who announces her at the woman he used to be with, the club's owner at him. The place has rules, hours, a payroll. That is what makes it usable: feeling moves through on a schedule, disguised as work, and nobody has to say anything. An auditor reads other people's lives in columns, and the club sells him the same procedure in the dark, with music. Toronto's festival named it the best Canadian film of its year and it holds a place on the TSPDT thousand. Its odd man out is a pet-shop owner, still at the edge of the arrangement, about to be drawn in.

In the story Ali grew up on, a sailor finds an island with two suns. He and Kwita, Omar and Boubker sleep on the Casablanca portside, get through the afternoons on glue, and keep clear of the gang they walked out on. Nabil Ayouch runs ninety-nine minutes on that arrangement and gives the island the same standing as the day's food and the day's hiding place, because for a boy who means to become a sailor they belong to one order of business. What stands to be lost is not only the four of them staying out of Dib's way. It is whether a private story can be kept intact by someone with nowhere to keep anything. The film was put forward as an international submission to the Academy Awards, which is an official sort of attention for four boys nobody had been counting.

The graves Guled digs are paying for the operation his wife needs. Nasra's kidneys are failing on their own schedule, the surgery has a price, and the two do not meet; the film is the distance between them. Khadar Ayderus Ahmed holds to eighty-three minutes and to one household on the outskirts of Djibouti city, husband and wife and a son old enough to hear what is being counted. Films built on poverty tend to run on incident. This one runs on a sum. The harder job is the marriage, since Guled and Nasra actually like each other, and affection is difficult to keep credible across conversation after conversation about cost, which is most of what they have to talk about. It carries two titles: one names her by his trade, the other just names them both.

Nobody came back to finish the towers after the government that started them ceased to exist. Two police officers find a burnt body in that half-built district, and then the shape of it begins to repeat, which is the worse discovery. Youssef Chebbi works in procedure, questions and corridors and a file, inside buildings that never acquired residents, so the case has to be assembled from evidence rather than from anyone's account of what they saw. A procedural usually runs on people who noticed something; here the concrete is the only witness on offer. Ninety-two minutes, in Arabic, 2022. The record we hold places it on the Étalon d'Or de Yennenga list. A thriller normally promises that a city can be read by someone patient enough, and these two are working the part of it that was never written down.

Ngando is an orphan, which in the arrangement he was born into is a financial condition before it is anything else. He and Ndomé want to marry, custom sets a dowry, and there is nobody behind him to pay it, so the request goes to his uncle, who understands precisely what it is worth. Jean-Pierre Dikongué-Pipa made this in Cameroon in 1975, ninety minutes, and the pressure in it is entirely domestic: no state, no court, nobody above the family to appeal to, because the family is the institution doing the damage. A love story usually needs an obstacle the couple can push against. Here the obstacle is a rule that everyone around them, including those who wish them well, holds to be correct. Two people are asked to want less, by an authority that never raises its voice.

It is a thriller first, with chases and danger and a deadline, and the thing being chased is a story about apartheid. Zola Maseko turns a hot-shot journalist loose in 1950s South Africa and lets the genre carry the load: ninety-four minutes, momentum, no lecture. A hot-shot is the right figure for it, the kind who keeps filing when caution would be the sensible course. Made in 2004, the film sits in our canon files on the Étalon d'Or de Yennenga list. What the structure buys is a clean view of the stakes, because the pleasures of an action picture, getting there first and getting out, are precisely what the work consists of when the rules are being rewritten around the man doing it. A reporter writes down what is happening, in a country organising itself so that what is happening cannot be written down.

Somewhere else the war continues; these two soldiers have lost their column. The Mercy of the Jungle is called a road movie, which is an odd thing to say about a jungle: no road, no map, no towns arriving in sequence, only the next few metres and whatever can be eaten. The wars in Congo are the subject and the film is the size of two men, rank and thirst and an argument about direction, the long business of staying alive while nothing gets decided. Ninety-one minutes, made in 2018. Joel Karekezi took the audience award at Rotterdam with it, which is a different kind of evidence from a jury prize: what holds a room here is not combat but whether two people with nothing left can still be of use to one another.

Old authority and new authority send their children to the same secondary school. Bah descends from a great chieftain; Batrou's father is a provincial military governor, which is where power has moved to. Neither chose the house they came from, and both are old enough now to be held to it. They meet as classmates in a generation with no intention of accepting either inheritance. Souleymane Cissé made it in Mali in 1982, a hundred minutes, in Bambara, and the friction runs two ways at once: students against the state, children against fathers, the same quarrel under two roofs that are supposed to be opposed. It took the Stallion of Yennenga and the Tanit d'or. What stands to be lost is not a regime. It is whether the young can refuse both fathers and still have anywhere to stand.

Testimony asks for a sequence, this happened and then this, and hands that work to whoever survived it. Ezra was taken as a boy by a rebel group; years later he has to give the account. Newton I. Aduaka takes a hundred and five minutes over it, with most of the weight falling on what a witness can actually retrieve and how much of that will be usable to the people listening. Two clocks run through the film, the one that recorded and the one that recalls, and they keep different time. A child soldier is a legal category before he is a person in a room. The gap between those is where this sits, since the hearing needs from him precisely the thing his years were arranged not to leave behind.

A man on the road tells the young factory manager that his family have always been servants to the manager's family. The manager gives him a job, and that decision is the hinge: looking out for one person puts him inside the accounts, where he begins to see what the company does to everyone else on the floor and what keeping his own position would cost. Souleymane Cissé shot it in Mali in 1978, in Bambara, ninety minutes. Industrial drama usually arrives with a clean line between management and labour; here the two share a street, a set of obligations and an inherited debt older than the factory. Our canon files list it under the Étalon d'Or de Yennenga. The pressure comes from other men's expectations, which are reasonable, constant and impossible to meet honestly.

Guimba rules a village in the Sahel, and the film about him is partly a comedy. Cheick Oumar Sissoko invented the place: a fictional village, a made-up reign, ninety-three minutes in 1995 on a chief and his son Jangine. A despot with an heir is a despot with a future, and the village has to live in it. The invention is the useful move. A real tyrant draws an argument about facts, while a fabricated one can be built to specification, given exactly the appetites the story needs, and laughed at without anyone reaching for the record. Comedy is not relief from the political material here. It is the instrument: what a tyranny looks like when its ceremonies are examined closely enough to turn absurd, and what it costs the people obliged to keep performing them.

His mother was killed as a witch, which the village has not forgotten now that his adopted sister has fallen ill. Wend Kuuni was raised by the family that took him in, and the charge against her has never quite come off him. Pughneere is sick; he sets out to find a healer, which is a rescue and a banishment at once. Gaston Kaboré places it in the early nineteenth century, ninety-seven minutes, and the journey works as a survey, since everyone met on the road is another answer to the question of what is owed a stranger. The accusation is the thing actually at stake. He can come back with a cure, but suspicion travels with him, and a village that has settled on something about a young man rarely unsettles it while he is away.

On 2 January 1899 a French column marched out of the French Sudan under two captains, and kept marching after the orders to stop had reached them. Med Hondo gave that campaign a hundred and twenty-two minutes in 1986 and set the queen of the Aznas against it. Sarraounia is a tactician and a practitioner of witchcraft, and the film refuses to treat those as separate competencies; both are methods for organising what people will do when they are frightened. The interest lies in the arithmetic of resistance, in what a small polity can mount against a force that has stopped answering to anyone, including the authority that sent it. At that length there is room for the distances and the waiting a campaign consists of. Colonial history, filmed from the side that had to plan for it.
